- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
> Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies,"according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices.
> "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies,"Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
> Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.
> Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.
> A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies,"the spokesperson said.
> "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,"Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.
> On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.
> "AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,"AMD said through a spokesperson.
> The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many,"Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.
> "It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly,"Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.
> The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
> The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal is the administration's first major personnel move since the outages.
> Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
> "The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
> Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the "honor of a lifetime to serve" in Trump's administration.
> The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.
> The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
> Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can "share with the American people what's happening here."
> Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature.
> Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.
> To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum.
> ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades).
> Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision.
> Yet knowing those upper limits doesnât tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, itâs hard to predict how capable a âgood enoughâ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human.
> What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both todayâs AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level A...

> The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17 per cent from its initial public offering price of US$83.
> Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares.
> To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles.

> Writing the largest check in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5 per cent, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion.
> To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies.
> Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets, joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars.
> Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first check at the start of this year, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February.
> It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab.

The announcement lists a speed of 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a context window of one million tokens, up from 260,000 tokens for Mercury 2.5. List pricing stands at $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.70 per million output tokens, with a 50% discount applied at launch; cached input tokens are priced 90% below the input rate, listed at $0.02 per million tokens and $0.01 under the promotion.
> Inception framed the release as evidence that text diffusion scales. According to the company, Mercury 3 is more than 40 times larger than Mercury 1 in total parameters, while intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks rose threefold from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. Inception described Mercury 1 as the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications and said the open question in the AI community had been whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases. The company said Mercury 3 answers that question, and that the scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion as well.
> Inception said early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 in latency-sensitive applications including browser-use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support. Shuhao Zhang, cofounder of TinyFish AI, said in the announcement that his company ran Mercury 3 inside its production web-agent harness against frontier models on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks, where Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, which he described as significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol, using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps at a fraction of the per-token cost.
> Michael Tong, co-founder and CTO of General Learning, known as RevisionDojo, said Mercury 3 let the tutoring company give every student instant feedback “without giving up reasoning,” with hints, marked answers, and definitions returning in about a second at q...

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
> An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhonemaker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
> Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
> “People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
> With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

> In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.
> One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:
> “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. > The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/0ffc162a6044e7c5
- Primary Source: CNBC (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/19/intuit-mailchimp-sale-bending-spoons.html)
- Executive Summary: Intuit has reached an agreement to sell its email-marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock, slated for closure in early 2027. This divestiture, representing a loss of over 70% from the $12 billion acquisition price in 2021, follows Mailchimp's stagnant revenue growth and its role as a drag on Intuit's broader financial valuation.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Intuit, Bending Spoons: Sale of Mailchimp for $3.68 billion, closing expected in early 2027
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Mailchimp's subpar revenue growth and lack of synergistic integration with core tax/accounting software

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Tax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.
> The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.
> The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.
> The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer.
> In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.
> Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue.
> While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.
> Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.
> The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.
> Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.

> President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offered little information about how he would steer the beleaguered agency during his confirmation hearing on Thursday.
> Michael LoSapio, the chief information security officer at the data analytics firm Palantir, provided only high-level answers to members of the Senate Homeland Security Committee who asked him how he would restore CISA’s ability to combat cyber threats after two years of Trump administration cuts.
> “I believe CISA is one of the only agencies in the government that plays a defensive cyber role in our nation,” LoSapio told Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who will chair the homeland-security panel in the next session of Congress.
> CISA’s “sole purpose is to provide resources [and] information to the defenders of state, local, and private entities for the purpose of cyber defense,” LoSapio continued. “If confirmed, I intend to bring together the community and the national labs to help collaborate and coordinate and to give defenders the tools they need to defend their networks.”
> LoSapio also described CISA as “the cybersecurity version of the 911 system” because of its role in responding to significant cyber incidents.
> But LoSapio, whose firm has extensive and controversial connections to the Trump administration, refused to weigh in on the administration’s downsizing of CISA, which has included mass layoffs and significant changes to the agency’s programs and services.
> “I can’t comment on the current state of CISA, because I’m not inside today,” he told Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.
> When Slotkin pressed LoSapio on whether he would support the Trump administration’s proposed $385 million cut to CISA’s budget, LoSapio again dodged the question.
> “I'm going to get involved and understand where the gaps are,” he said, “and I will come back to this committee with a gap analysis.”
> Slotkin said LoSapio was too afraid of angering Trump to be an effective CISA director.
> “You should be able to say clearly, there’s increasing threat, therefore we need increasing resources to deal with it,” she said, “and the fact that you can’t say that means that you’re more worried about the political ramifications than you are about the national security of the country.”
> “I don’t necessarily believe more money means more security,” LoSapio responded. “I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk.”
> At other times, LoSapio appeared unprepared to discuss the details of CISA’s work. When Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., asked him what his top priorities would be as CISA’s director, he gave a vague answer that did not mention...

> ### Evasive and irregular turns

> Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

Prosecutors said the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.
> Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.
> It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.
> Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> AI has an image problem, to say the least, with public fears on the rise that the technology could lead to mass unemployment and human extinction. So for its new AI agent Muse and an associated device, Meta is dialing down the fear factor and cranking up the cute. To sell AI hardware to the masses, Meta is going kawaii.
> Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the company's forthcoming Muse Charm on Wednesday, a handheld device for its new AI agent. It looks like a futuristic Tamagotchi and personifies the chatbot on the screen as a fuzzy, rotund beige mascot. You can name the creature yourself.
> Instagram's Adam Mosseri named his "Max." (Facebook and Instagram introduced their users to the avatar this week to entice downloads of the Muse app.) "We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to," Zuckerberg said at Meta Connect.
> Instead of visualizing its new AI agent as non-anthropromorphic glowing orb, like Siri, or a cursor and text, like ChatGPT, Muse is a cute monster avatar. Meta could have gone down the route of its competitors, but it didn't. Instead its choice shows something about how big tech is appealing to softer emotions in the race toward mass adoption.
> The Muse agent can read emails, book classes, draft documents, and make purchases (just not on Amazon, which blocked it). That cross-platform functionality means allowing Muse access to a lot of accounts, which requires trust—something Meta and social media companies at large struggle with.
> If Muse and the Muse Charm are successful, however, it could prove that a mascot-led brand approach does a better job countering consumer AI fears than a disembodied voice or orb. The cuteness factor has shown up in transportation recently with vehicles like Robotaxi Zoox, Amazon delivery vans, and the DoorDash Dot delivery robot.
> The vehicles are rounded in shape and designed to look non-intimidating. The trend is towards taking technology that might otherwise be seen as threatening, like autonomous vehicles or AI, and giving a friendly, charming exterior. Cuteness, research has shown, also sparks a caregiving response—quite the opposite from the feelings of fear and concern that many Americans have about AI.
> While you can use Muse on a smartphone, Zuckerberg explained the Muse Charm as something you use without having to unlock a phone or open an app. It's a fun novelty that could find early adopters among people looking for a device that reduces their screentime. Zuckerberg said materials and components are being finalized for the Muse Charm and there isn't yet a price tag for the device, but the company plans to be ready to ship in time for the holidays.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> US companies are using AI models more intensively than ever and paying less for the privilege.
> The latest update of the Ramp AI Index, which draws on transaction data from more than 85,000 US companies, lays out the numbers. Tokens, the units of computation in which AI providers bill model usage, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, according to Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian. At the same time, token volume rose 1.5 percent to a record high.
> Token spending, meaning what companies actually pay for AI APIs, fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier. Month over month (the week ending November 15 vs. the week ending October 18), total token spending still rose 12 percent, but token volume jumped 27.2 percent over the same span. The gap between usage and revenue keeps widening.
> The average price per million tokens for OpenAI and Anthropic combined fell to $0.45, according to Ramp, down 11.2 percent from the prior month. OpenAI is cheaper at $0.38 per million tokens compared with $0.50 for Anthropic.
> API routing platform OpenRouter shows a similar pattern. According to an analysis Peter Walker published on X, weekly token volume for closed-weight models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google grew 1,215 percent since the start of 2026. Weekly spending rose 455 percent over the same period, far more slowly. The spending peak came in the week of October 5, according to the OpenRouter data, which runs through the week of November 9. Spending has been declining since then.
> Ramp's token metrics rely on usage and billing data imported from AI providers, while OpenRouter measures traffic through its API routing platform. The fact that both sources show a spending peak in October followed by declining outlays and rising volume reinforces the trend, though neither service is representative of the overall market. OpenRouter in particular offers only a narrow window into a very specific user base.
> ### Anthropic dominates the token market on IPO day
> In the week ending November 15, 2026, Anthropic accounted for 58.7 percent of all token spending, according to the Ramp AI Index, up 1.7 percentage points from the prior month. Its share of token volume was even higher at 59.4 percent. OpenAI fell to 37.2 percent of spending and 37.7 percent of volume. Google came in at 1.4 percent and xAI (SpaceXAI) at 2.4 percent.
> Kharazian wrote on X that Anthropic holds this share on IPO day. In October, however, Anthropic's token spending grew only 0.5 percent month over month, while OpenAI's grew 2.1 percent.
> In October 2026, 56.8 percent of all tracked US companies paid for AI products or services, according to Ramp, up one percentage point from September and 13.3 percentage points more than a year earlier. Anthropic leads with an adoption rate of 44.8 percent, while ...

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> A bipartisan coalition of over two dozen House lawmakers is forming a new artificial intelligence caucus. The group, dubbed the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, will be led by Reps. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas).
> It will seek to balance creating AI safeguards that mitigate the technology’s risks with “ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies,” according to an announcement first shared with POLITICO. The group’s creation comes as lawmakers look ahead to the next Congress and grapple with Washington's role in governing the emerging technology.
> “We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides, who is positioning himself as a prominent voice on AI in Congress, said in an interview. He said the group would work to create, give feedback on and endorse legislation.
> Other groups tend to focus more on educating members or working on legislation with colleagues of their own party, leaving a gap for a bipartisan coalition like his. They would also make a concerted effort to engage in “rapid response” to AI incidents and breaches, which other caucuses have been less engaged in, he said.
> When incidents occur and the public questions whether to attribute it to AI, like the outage of major infrastructure that Americans experienced the past week in the country’s air traffic control systems or Microsoft Outlook, the group will leverage their contacts across industry, safety groups, the intelligence community and other government agencies to gather information.
> “We want to begin to communicate to the American public that Congress can move at a pace that is responsive to the pace of AI change,” said Whitesides, a former chief of staff at NASA. Whitesides’ push is joining a crowded field of other AI-focused bodies that have formed in Congress.
> Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries formed an AI commission chaired by three Democrats tasked with charting the caucus’ future on AI policy. The Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus, co-chaired by four lawmakers, including Beyer, has been focused on educating members on the technology, Whitesides said.
> In contrast, his group will try to take a more active voice in tech policy on the Hill. Democrats have also debated creating a select committee on AI. But the idea has faced opposition from some lawmakers poised to chair committees that oversee AI policy, The trio of chairs will be joined by California Democrats Sara Jacobs, Ro Khanna, Sam Liccardo, Ted Lieu, Zoe Lofgren, Brad Sherman, Doris Matsui and Scott Peters alongside Greg Casar (D-Texas), Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), Ben Cline (R-Va.), Mike F...

- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/3e5557b0c0cc7405

This feature is gated behind Gemini Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscriptions and is currently limited to English users in the U.S., requiring explicit user approval for agentic actions via a live preview interface.

By leveraging macOS as a premium productivity touchpoint, Google aims to enhance subscription retention; however, until cross-application semantic understanding reaches a higher threshold of reliability, this remains a sophisticated assistive tool rather than a fully autonomous workflow engine.'}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
> The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.
> Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
> Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.
> As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.
> Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.
> The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
> The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.
> Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.
> Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.
> Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.
> The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.
> “We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”
> Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.
> Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.

### Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/9ab20d78281035e1
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/tech/1037902/google-gemini-macos-ai-computer-use)
- Executive Summary: Google has introduced the "Computer Use" feature to its Gemini app for macOS, enabling the AI to execute multi-step tasks across local files, desktop applications, and the web. Currently rolling out in the US, the feature allows users to designate app access while monitoring AI actions through a real-time background preview window.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Google (macOS environment): Deployed AI Agent with capabilities to operate local apps and web interfaces
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To increase productivity via workflow automation and secure system-level AI integration

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says. Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale.
> Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US.
> Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.
> Days after the US Commerce Department closed the cloud loophole for AI chips in the wake of the scandal around former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the fallout in Asia's tech industry is immediate. Chinese firms had been skirting US sanctions by renting compute capacity in third countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Those data centers now need a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that regulates sensitive technologies and enforces US export controls. Existing operators have a 90-day transition period and must rigorously screen their customers for ties to China.
> According to the law firm Sidley Austin, the licensing requirement kicks in at an extremely low threshold equivalent to roughly 300 modern AI chips, while Chinese labs typically need several thousand processors. The Information reports that Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI canceled a $150 million contract with a Southeast Asian cloud provider in Indonesia in response and paused talks on additional deals.
> Moonshot had planned to rent a large cluster of Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips there starting next year to train its next language model, Kimi K4. Because of the heavy compute demand, the company had agreed to prepay about 50 percent instead of the industry-standard 15 percent. Access to Blackwell chips abroad was already critical for its predecessor model K3, which matched top US models in July and triggered a BIS investigation, The Information also reported.
> Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin are warning of rising training costs, and banks are pulling back too. According to Bloomberg, five lenders are considering dropping out of a $480 million loan for Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which was supposed to supply Nvidia chips in Malaysia for TikTok parent ByteDance.
> ### TSMC and Samsung halt chip shipments to China
> Beyond cloud restrictions, the new US rules are also starting to cut physical supply chains. The Financial Times reports that contract manufacturers TSMC and Samsung stopped certain processor shipments to Chinese customers in recent days while they apply for Commerce Department licenses. The move hits Chinese tech firms at a time when they are already struggling with historically high memory chip prices and capacity bottlenecks at domestic foundries such as SMIC. Huawei recently told its customers to source their own memory for its new AI chip.
> The new BIS rules block a workaround through independent packaging and testing firms that Chinese chip de...

This sandbox hosts realistic versions of social media, e-commerce, and banking platforms, allowing researchers to evaluate the resilience of Gemini-powered web-browsing agents against prompt-injection attacks and other real-world vulnerabilities without risking the open web.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.
> “Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.
> The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.
> “Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”
> Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.
> Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity ch...

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nov 19 (Reuters) - Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO brings to Wall Street an avatar of a sector that proponents herald as an economic panacea, while detractors warn it has stoked a market bubble and could ultimately threaten humanity itself.
> More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker's debut after securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in the IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.
> The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to the sector, even as a rocky market reception for Nvidia results which looked strong at first blush, signals the euphoria around the sector has cooled.
> "I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.
> AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.
> Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the incipient crushing debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.
> An extramarital-affair scandal involving Nvidia's CEO and a spike in Treasury yields have further unnerved investors.
> As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.
> The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the roadshow. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion.
> "Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
> London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive demand from index-tracking funds will account for about 28% of Anthropic's shares offered, or roughly $19 billion.
> When it debuts on the Nasdaq later on Thursday, Anthropic will join the world's trillion-dollar club, alongside technology giants such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.
> The listing will also give retail investors a chance to pile into one of the AI industry's hottest names, potentially amplifying swings in the stock as trading begins.
> The buzz has already spilled onto prediction markets, where traders are placing bets on everything fro...
